newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank adopts reserve system reform.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank adopts reserve system reform.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank on Thursday approved a scheme to liberalise the island's bank reserve system, striving to bring it in line with international practices, bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said.
Taiwan has said it would adjust the limits on banks' reserve requirements as part of a bid to join the World Trade Organisation.

Under current law, range limits are set for banks' reserve requirements -- with 15-40 percent for checking deposits, 10-35 percent for passbook deposits, five to 20 percent for savings deposits and seven to 25 percent for time deposits.
Sheu, disclosing details of the reform package to reporters after a bank board meeting, said the bank would gradually lower banks' reserve requirements "at the appropriate time".
He gave no timetable for the adjustments, but said the strategy was in line with international trends toward lower reserve requirements.
Sheu said the central bank's long-term goal was that Taiwan's financial institutions ultimately would be free to determine their own reserve levels.
Sheu said the board agreed to leave reserve requirements unchanged at Thursday's meeting, saying board members wanted to maintain the current "stable-to-loose" monetary policy.
Sheu said the bank would conduct open-market operations in order to maintain financial stability, but gave no details.

The central bank has maintained a similar monetary policy for weeks, trying to strike a balance that keeps interest rates low enough to stimulate the flagging economy without undermining the interests of bank depositors.
